title: Afanasy Nikitin's Journey Beyond Three Seas
intro: Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant from Tver, set out on a trading trip planned for the lands around the Caspian Sea as far as Shirvan. Robbed on the way, he went on through Persia and reached India, where he spent almost three years. The dates are debated: scholars long gave 1466 to 1472, but Leonid Semyonov reconstructed 1468 to 1474.
ending: Nikitin sailed home by way of Muscat and Trabzon and across the Black Sea to Caffa, where he most likely composed his narrative. He died near Smolensk in the spring of 1475, and other Russian merchants took his notes to Moscow, where they were included in state chronicles.

legs.title: Down the Volga and the Caspian

stops.text: Nikitin, son of Nikita and a merchant of Tver, left his home town on a commercial trip. He planned to trade around the Caspian Sea and go as far as Shirvan.
stops.quote: In 1466 or 1468, Nikitin left his hometown of Tver on a commercial trip, planning to trade in the lands around the Caspian Sea and go as far as Shirvan (in modern-day Azerbaijan).

stops.text: Nikitin travelled down the Volga, passing Uglich, Kostroma and Plyos, and reached Nizhny Novgorod. There he and his fellow merchants followed the caravan of Hasan Beg, the returning ambassador from Shirvan, further south.
stops.quote: Following the caravan of the returning ambassador to Moscow from Shirvan, Hasan Beg, Nikitin and his fellow merchants traveled further south.

stops.text: Near Astrakhan the party was attacked and robbed by Nogais, whom Nikitin calls Tatars. It was robbed again by Kaitags on the Caspian coast, and some of the Russian merchants were taken prisoner.
stops.quote: Near Astrakhan, his party was attacked and robbed first by Nogais (whom he calls Tatars), then again by Kaitags on the Caspian coast.

stops.text: Nikitin went to the Shirvanshah's camp to plead for help. The ruler freed the captives but refused the means to return home, and the party dispersed, some going back to Rus and some to work at Baku.
stops.quote: Nikitin went to the Shirvanshah's (the ruler of Shirvan) camp in Shemakha to plead for help.

stops.text: Hoping to recoup his losses, Nikitin went on to Derbent, which was a familiar market to him.
stops.quote: Hoping to recoup his losses, Nikitin continued on to Derbent, which was a familiar market to him, and then to Baku.

stops.text: From Baku Nikitin crossed the Caspian Sea into Persia, where he followed a known trade route and made prolonged stops in market towns.
stops.quote: He then crossed the Caspian Sea into Persia, where he followed a known trade route and made prolonged stops in market towns.

legs.title: Across Persia and the sea to India

stops.text: After Chapakur, Sari, Amol, Kashan and Yazd, Nikitin reached Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, having spent two years in Persia. Muslim merchants had told him of the riches of India, and he sailed for India from Hormuz.
stops.quote: In the spring of 1471, Nikitin sailed for India from Hormuz and, after making several stops, arrived in the port of Chaul six weeks later.

stops.text: Nikitin arrived at the port of Chaul six weeks after leaving Hormuz. It was probably after his arrival in India that he began writing his travel notes.
stops.quote: It was probably after his arrival in India that he began writing his travel notes.

stops.text: Nikitin described the rainy season while living in Junnar, when for four months there was water and mud everywhere, by day and by night.
stops.quote: He described the rainy season while living in Junnar, when "throughout four months there was water and mud everywhere, both by day and at night.

stops.text: In the third year of his journey Nikitin wrote that at Bidar, the Bahmani capital, he shed many tears for the Christian faith. He had lost contact with Christianity and lived among Muslims.
stops.quote: He also wrote that at Bindar in the third year of his journey he "shed many tears for the Christian faith".

stops.text: After almost three years in India, Nikitin decided to return to Russia, concluding that further travel would bring him no great profit. On the way back he visited Muscat.
stops.quote: On his way back, Nikitin visited Muscat, the Arabian sultanate of Somalia, and Trabzon.

stops.text: Nikitin visited Trabzon, also written Trebizond, and in November 1474 sailed from there to Caffa.
stops.quote: In November 1474, he sailed from Trebizond to Caffa (now Feodosia), where there was a large Russian settlement.

stops.text: Caffa, now Feodosia, had a large Russian settlement. It is most likely that Nikitin composed his narrative here from his travel notes and memories.
stops.quote: It is most likely in Caffa that he composed Khozheniye za tri morya on the basis of his travel notes and memories.

stops.text: On his way to Tver Nikitin died not far from Smolensk. Other Russian merchants took his notes to Vasily Mamyrev, secretary to Ivan III, grand prince of Moscow.
stops.quote: On his way to Tver, Nikitin died not far from Smolensk in the spring of 1475.

notes: Dates: the article says 1466 or 1468 for the departure and, per Semyonov, India 1471-1474 (older view 1466-1472); undated Russian and Caspian stops carry 'the departure year' as a placeholder. Muscat has no date in the article (1471 is a placeholder; it is after the almost three years in India, so likely 1474 on Semyonov's chronology). Junnar and Bidar order is inferred (Bidar 'third year'); the article does not order them. Hormuz wp is Hormuz Island (medieval city location uncertain). Left out: Makaryev Monastery, Uglich, Kostroma, Plyos (passed only), Chapakur, Sari, Amol, Kashan, Yazd (passed, no event; Chapakur six months but no article place), Parvattum (no article), Calicut, Dabhol, Cambay, Bidar trade remarks (trade only), Somalia. Trabzon visit is before the November 1474 sailing; same stop.
